blocks.md: Changing variables means re-expressing a problem in more convenient units — say, working with log wages instead of wages. When you stretch or squeeze the axis, probabilities have to be rescaled so they still add up to one, and that rescaling factor is the key to getting densities right. It explains, for example, why the average wage is higher than the wage of a typical worker when log wages follow a bell curve.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is how you derive the distribution of any transformed variable, and why exponentiating a predicted log does not give the predicted average.

In many dimensions the factor becomes $|\det J|$, the absolute determinant of the Jacobian matrix of the transformation ([Invertibility and Determinants](note:invertibility-and-determinants)) — how much the map stretches volume.
Probability is conserved; the Jacobian factor corrects for stretching the axis.
Wages are often modelled as lognormal: $\ln W = Z \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$. With $W = e^Z$, $g^{-1}(w) = \ln w$ and $dg^{-1}/dw = 1/w$:

and its mean is $E[W] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$, not $e^{\mu}$ (which is the median). With $\mu = 3$, $\sigma = 0.5$: $E[W] = 22.76$ while $e^3 = 20.09$. The gap grows with $\sigma^2$, the [Variance of Log Income](note:variance-of-log-income): more inequality, larger mean–median gap. This is [Convexity and Concavity](note:convexity-and-concavity) (Jensen) made exact.

- Forgetting the Jacobian factor, so the density no longer integrates to 1.
- Forgetting the absolute value when $g$ is decreasing.
- Exponentiating a predicted $\ln y$ and calling it the predicted mean of $y$.
